content: The Antonine Plague, which occurred between 165 and 180 CE, is also referred to as the Plague of Galen. This pandemic, believed to have been caused by either smallpox or measles, was introduced to the Roman Empire by soldiers returning from military campaigns in the Near East. The epidemic was responsible for the deaths of two Roman emperors: Lucius Verus, who succumbed to the disease in 169 CE, and his co-ruler Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who ruled until his death in 180 CE. The epidemic was named after Marcus Aurelius's family name, Antoninus. According to the Roman historian Dio Cassius, the disease re-emerged nine years after its initial outbreak, causing up to 2,000 deaths per day in Rome, which accounted for one-quarter of those infected. The total death toll from the epidemic is estimated to have reached five million. During the epidemic in 166 CE, the Greek physician Galen, who was also a prolific writer, left Rome and returned to his home in Asia Minor. However, he was summoned back to Rome in 168 CE by the two emperors. Galen documented his observations of the epidemic in his treatise Methodus Medendi, though his descriptions were brief. He noted symptoms such as fever, diarrhea, inflammation of the pharynx, and a skin eruption that could be either dry or pustular, typically appearing on the ninth day of illness. Despite Galen's accounts, the exact nature of the disease remains unclear, though most scholars have identified it as smallpox. The Antonine Plague had profound social and political consequences for the Roman Empire. When the Parthian king Vologases IV launched an attack on Armenia, Roman forces, led by Emperor Verus, moved east to defend the territory. However, the epidemic severely weakened the Roman military, as large numbers of soldiers fell ill. According to the 4th-century writer Paulus Orosius, entire towns and villages in Italy and other European provinces were depopulated. The disease also spread beyond the Empire's borders, infecting Germanic and Gallic tribes to the north. These groups, who had been migrating southward in search of land, encountered weakened Roman defenses due to the epidemic. From 167 CE until his death, Marcus Aurelius personally led Roman legions along the Danube River, attempting to halt the advance of Germanic tribes. However, a major offensive against the Marcomanni was delayed until 169 CE due to a shortage of troops. During this time, Marcus Aurelius composed his philosophical work Meditations, in which he reflected on the epidemic, stating in Passage IX.2 that the pestilence was less harmful than falsehood, immoral behavior, and ignorance. As he lay dying from the disease, Marcus Aurelius reportedly said, Weep not for me; think rather of the pestilence and the deaths of so many others. The Plague of Cyprian, which occurred between 251 and 266 CE, marked another devastating outbreak of disease. At its peak, it was reported that 5,000 people were dying each day in Rome. Cyprian, the bishop of Carthage, described the plague in his essay De mortalitate (On Mortality) and used the epidemic as a moral lesson in his sermons to the Christian community. His biographer, Pontius the deacon, documented the impact of the plague in Carthage. During this time, Christians were scapegoated for the epidemic, much like Jews were during the Black Death in the 14th century. The Decian persecution, which coincided with the onset of the plague, targeted Christians as a response to the crisis. Fifty years later, Arnobius, a North African convert to Christianity, defended the religion against pagan accusations that it was responsible for the plague. Historian William McNeill has suggested that the Antonine Plague and the Plague of Cyprian were caused by two distinct diseases, likely smallpox and measles, though the order of their occurrence is uncertain.
